script.title: Why Maya ground still holds mercury

lines: A Maya family buried their dead right inside their own home compound.
For the Maya, the land was the property of the ancestors.
Burying the dead at home tied each family to its land.
And for funerals, the Classic Maya used a stone called cinnabar.
Cinnabar is a mercury material.
Archaeologists report extensive deposits of cinnabar in ancient settlements.
In important burials, they even found rare traces of pure liquid mercury.
Then, by about the 10th century, the great cities were abandoned.
The families walked away.
The mercury did not.
You see, it's like a stain on a carpet.
The guests go home.
The stain stays.
Scientists compared mercury readings from ten ancient Maya settlements.
Seven sites from ten had at least one spot that equals or exceeds modern toxic limits.
The high mercury is typically found where Maya people once lived.
It most likely came from their cinnabar.
The Maya buried their dead to bind them to the land.
Their mercury stayed bound to the land too.
Now scientists want to know what it did to people's health.

claims.claim: Clans held that the land was the property of the ancestors, and ties between the land and the ancestors were reinforced by the burial of the dead within residential compounds.
The Classic Period Maya used mercury for decorative and ceremonial (including funerary) purposes, cinnabar predominantly.
Archaeologists have reported extensive deposits of cinnabar in ancient settlements, and rare finds of elemental mercury in important burial and religious contexts.
The locations with elevated mercury are typically former Maya occupation areas in large urban settlements abandoned by c. 10th century CE.
Seven sites from ten reported at least one location with mercury concentrations that equal or exceed modern benchmarks for environmental toxicity.
The mercury detected in buried contexts at Maya sites is most likely associated with pre-Columbian mercury use, especially of cinnabar.
Researchers call for interpreting environmental mercury data in the context of mercury exposure and human health at Maya sites.

cast.father: a 40 year old Maya farmer, lean and wiry, dark copper skin, a long sloping forehead, a hooked nose, clean shaven, long black hair tied in a topknot with a white cloth band, a white cotton loincloth and a short red and black woven cape, 800s
cast.mother: a 35 year old Maya woman, short and sturdy, a round face with warm brown skin and full cheeks, long black hair wrapped in a mustard yellow woven headband, a white cotton huipil tunic with red diamond embroidery and a dark blue wrap skirt, 800s
cast.archaeologist: a 58 year old woman archaeologist, tall and thin, a deeply tanned lined face, short spiky silver hair, no glasses, a dusty pale blue denim work shirt with rolled sleeves and a wide brimmed straw sun hat, today
cast.scientist: a 41 year old Latino environmental scientist, stocky, a shaved head, a short black goatee, thick black eyebrows, a sun faded orange field shirt, khaki cargo trousers and a grey bucket hat, today

shots.name: hook
shots.prompt: medium shot, a Maya man lowering a body wrapped in white cotton into a pit dug in the earth floor of a house courtyard, he is {father}, warm late afternoon light
shots.motion: he slowly lowers the wrapped body, slow camera push in
shots.check: Is a man lowering a wrapped body into a pit?

shots.name: compound

shots.check: Are there small houses with thatched roofs?

shots.motion: she presses her palms into the soil, slow camera push in
shots.check: Is a woman pressing her hands on the soil?
